p.title: Influence maximization in social networks: a survey of behaviour-aware methods

ext.title: Influence maximization in social networks: a survey of behaviour-aware methods
ext.venue: Social Network Analysis and Mining, 13:78 (published online 25 April 2023; received 23 May 2022, revised 12 March 2023, accepted 27 March 2023)
ext.document_type: Review paper (literature survey with a proposed taxonomy; no empirical study)
ext.coverage: Read the full extracted text (all 2,484 lines, about 114k characters, in seven chunks), including front matter, Sections 1 to 4, all four summary tables (Tables 1 to 4, rendered as check-mark grids), author contributions, declarations and the full reference list (pp. 18-21). The metadata hint is correct on title, authors, year, venue and DOI. The text does not discuss lobbying, elections, legislators, text measurement or turnout; the closest content is money-aware (cost and budget) and opinion-aware (trust, opinion) seed selection, covered below. No Paul markup exists: the _annots and annotations folders contain no file matching 0bc326441250, so paul_markup is empty.
ext.research_question: No empirical question is posed. The paper asks what behaviour-aware methods for influence maximization (IM) exist in social networks, and proposes to classify and review them as a separate family from behaviour-agnostic, purely structural methods (Sec. 1, pp. 1-3). It also states that previous surveys covered behaviour-agnostic approaches or touched behaviour-aware ones only briefly (p. 2).
ext.theory: No formal social or economic theory is tested. The framing is IM as discrete optimisation (Eq. 1, p. 4): select a seed set S of size k or under budget B that maximises spread phi(S), with query Q = (M, AM, B) and graph G = (V, E, BV, BE). Behaviour-aware methods use user features BV, relationship features BE and message features AM. Diffusion models are Independent Cascade and Linear Threshold (Kempe et al. 2003; Granovetter 1978), with voter and opinion-formation models used for opinion dynamics.
ext.data: None. This is a narrative review with no sample, unit of analysis, N or data period. Cited works span roughly 1977 to 2023, but the paper states no explicit inclusion window or search protocol.
ext.method: Narrative classification and review. The authors propose a two-level taxonomy (pp. 2-5, Fig. 2). Level 1 splits IM methods into behaviour-agnostic and behaviour-aware. Level 2 splits behaviour-aware methods into four families: interest-aware (target-aware, label-aware, topic-aware; Sec. 3.1), opinion-aware (trust-agnostic, trust-aware; Sec. 3.2), money-aware (cost-aware, profit-aware; Sec. 3.3) and physical-world-aware (physical relationship-aware, location-aware; Sec. 3.4). Summary tables code each surveyed paper by behavioural features (AM, BV, BE), influence-detection method (centrality measure CM, spreading simulation SS, reverse influence sampling RIS, maximum influence arborescence MIA) and spreading process type (simple or complex). Section 2.2 ranks influence-detection families by time complexity: simulation-based, then MIA, then RIS, then centrality (p. 4).
ext.identification: Not applicable. The paper makes no causal or statistical identification claim. It classifies published methods and does not estimate effects.
ext.scope: Population: social-network IM research, covering online graphs (friendship, follow, trust) and, for physical-world-aware methods, check-in and location-based social networks (Sec. 3.4). No institution or era restriction beyond the cited literature. Behaviour-agnostic methods are explicitly excluded as already surveyed elsewhere (pp. 3, 5).

key_findings.finding: Behaviour-agnostic methods dominate current IM work because they have a longer history, but behaviour-aware formulations are argued to be more realistic. No previous survey had treated behaviour-aware methods as a class of their own.

Interest-aware methods split into target-aware (binary interest), label-aware (label sets) and topic-aware (continuous topic vectors). Topic-aware models are judged to capture preferences most realistically but need good historical records. Partly offline topic-aware methods trade offline storage and precomputation for faster online queries.
key_findings.numbers: Table 1 codes the interest-aware papers; no numeric results

key_findings.finding: Opinion-aware methods split into trust-agnostic (all ties positive) and trust-aware (signed friend or foe ties). Trust-agnostic models assume all relationships are positive, which the authors call unrealistic; opinion dynamics under friend and foe influence need more work.
key_findings.numbers: None; Table 2 codes the opinion-aware papers

key_findings.finding: Cost-aware (budgeted) IM assumes every activated user yields the same benefit. Profit-aware methods model per-user benefit and cost, but users' valuations may often be unavailable, so the authors suggest cost-aware methods may be more practical.
key_findings.numbers: Nguyen and Zheng (2013) introduced budgeted IM; Table 3 codes the money-aware papers

key_findings.finding: Physical-world-aware methods add offline ties (co-location, check-in) to the online graph, or use location and attendance probability as the target. Binary physical-tie models and fixed distance thresholds miss the dynamics of user location, and tracking locations over time adds processing and storage cost.

Five open challenge areas are identified: data availability, data processing, data modelling (numeric encodings of attitude and friend or foe ties), data dynamicity, and user reaction modelling. Research directions cover network size and time complexity, network diversity (temporal, multilayer, dynamic), data preparation, and adaptive diffusion models that feed behaviour changes back into spread.

measures: Not applicable to the paper's own analysis. Reviewed methods use centrality measures, spreading simulation, reverse influence sampling (Borgs et al. 2012) and maximum influence arborescence (Chen et al. 2010). Tables 1-4 code features as AM, BV, BE and detection as CM, SS, RIS or MIA, with simple or complex spreading.
limitations: The paper states no methodological limitations of its own review: no search protocol, inclusion rule, or count of surveyed papers.
Stated scope limit: it reviews behaviour-aware methods only and defers behaviour-agnostic methods to earlier surveys (pp. 3, 5).
Stated challenge: behaviour data may not exist, may be incomplete or noisy, or may be governed by privacy rules (Sec. 4, p. 17).
Stated challenge: many behaviour-aware models encode attitudes and friend or foe ties as numbers, which may not capture personality or attitude (Sec. 4, p. 17).
Stated challenge: most methods use conventional IC or LT diffusion models that may not emulate real spreading; changing the model can significantly change accuracy (Sec. 4, p. 18).
The paper classifies methods and does not benchmark or compare their accuracy.
references_of_note: Kempe, Kleinberg and Tardos (2003), first discrete-optimisation formulation of IM; basis of IC and LT models

rel.summary_md:
Zareie and Sakellariou (2023, SNAM 13:78) is a narrative survey with no data. It proposes a two-level taxonomy of influence maximization (IM). Level 1 separates behaviour-agnostic methods, which use structure only, from behaviour-aware methods. Level 2 splits behaviour-aware methods into four families: interest-aware (target, label, topic), opinion-aware (trust-agnostic vs signed friend/foe), money-aware (cost-aware budgeted IM vs profit-aware) and physical-world-aware. Tables 1-4 code each surveyed method by which features it uses: message (AM), user (BV) or relationship (BE). They also code how it detects influence (centrality, simulation, RIS or MIA) and whether spreading is simple or complex. The useful content is qualitative. Topic-aware edge probabilities are judged the most realistic, but they need rich history. Trust-agnostic models, which treat every tie as positive, are called unrealistic. Profit-aware IM needs per-user valuations that are rarely available, so cost-aware IM may be more practical. The authors also warn that changing the diffusion model can change accuracy a lot, and that many users are silent.

For Melange the paper is mainly a lens on design choices that were already made. The code cites it directly: receptivity_layer.py:29-31 and outcome_contract.py:17 ('Chen/SNAM') use it to back contingency-aware seeding. But the survey gives no estimate of seed take-up and no magnitudes, so it supports only the general idea that member features belong in IM. Against the built engine, the survey exposes three choices. First, one topic-independent cascade kernel serves all 18 CU categories. Second, the kernel is trust-agnostic: partisan factors change edge magnitude, never sign, and the signed reference layer is display-only. Third, the optimizer has a profit-aware shape, weighting members by owner-set values (PERS, IMP), which is the exact data the survey calls usually unavailable. All of these are design-level bearings. Nothing in the paper validates or refutes any constant in the system.

bearings.paper_claim: Behaviour-aware IM adds user features (BV), relationship features (BE) and message features (AM) to the structural seed-selection problem (Eq. 1, query Q=(M, AM, B)). The survey reports no take-up rate, no effect size and no benchmark: it 'classifies methods and does not benchmark'. It also warns that numeric encodings of attitude may not capture personality, and that many users are silent.
bearings.system_side: gate(n) = max(0.15, seed_prob(n) x SGATE[tier]). seed_prob = clip(0.60 + .10 coop + .06 breadth + .04 visibility, 0.30, 0.90) on the behavioural basis (A/O/E on the lexical basis). The docstring cites 'Chen et al. (UAI 2021) + the behaviour-aware IM survey (Zareie & Sakellariou SNAM 2023)' as the basis. The H1 contract is labelled 'Chen/SNAM'.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Supports only the framing that member attributes may enter seed activation. It does not support the 0.60 baseline, the trait or behaviour coefficients, or the 0.30-0.90 clip, which are design priors. The survey covers online social graphs (friendship, follow, trust), not legislators being lobbied. H1 (Spearman of seed_prob vs new cosponsorship, which needs at least 150 movers; F5 found 72) is the only route to evidence. Until it is scored, the seed_prob magnitudes stay unvalidated.

bearings.paper_claim: Topic-aware IM (Barbieri, Bonchi and Manco 2013) makes influence probabilities depend on the message's topic vector. The authors judge it the most realistic interest-aware formulation, but say it needs good historical records. Partly offline variants trade precomputation and storage for faster queries.
bearings.system_side: Every per-topic engine builds the same topic-independent kernel, P = build_P(load_network()), from the CU cosponsor graph. Topics differ only in target weights (IMP, PERS, engagement) and in industry money, never in edge probabilities. Sector graphs (bank_reg, crypto) exist as separate NET_CONFIGs but are not used per CU category.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Transfers only if per-category cosponsorship history is dense enough to estimate topic-specific edge weights. The recorded crypto p_max of 0.23, below the engine floor, suggests thin categories would fail. Any topic-conditioned kernel would also change ranks and engine outputs, so change-control applies. The survey reports no accuracy gain over topic-blind IM, so the benefit is conjectural.

bearings.paper_claim: Trust-agnostic opinion-aware models assume every relationship is positive, which the authors call unrealistic. Trust-aware models use signed friend/foe ties (Li, Chen, Wang and Zhang 2013), on the premise that 'opinion change depends on the trust between the users'. The authors also note that numeric friend/foe encodings may not capture attitudes, and that IC/LT may not emulate real spreading; changing the model can change accuracy significantly.
bearings.system_side: p(u->v) = x/(x+6), with x = w x cpf x edge_mult(v). cpf_diffusion (0.4-1.0) and cpf_pressure (1.7/0.5) change edge magnitude by party, but every edge stays positive, so the kernel is trust-agnostic in the survey's terms. The signed member-reference layer (LLM valence) is display-only and does not feed the kernel.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This is a design taxonomy, not evidence that signed edges improve prediction in Congress. Any foe-edge adoption would need a second path showing that negative references or signed-backbone ties predict lower future cosponsorship (DE-062). The survey's own warning about numeric attitude encodings applies to the LLM valence scores. It would also break the 'two cpf physics, never merge' architecture, so this is owner policy.

bearings.paper_claim: Cost-aware (budgeted) IM (Nguyen and Zheng 2013) assumes every activated user yields the same benefit. Profit-aware IM (Lu and Lakshmanan 2012) models per-user benefit and cost, but users' valuations are often unavailable, so the authors suggest cost-aware methods may be more practical.
bearings.system_side: CELF lazy greedy spends a $2.5M pot in $500 chunks (PMAX $10k) to maximize separable winnability, sum of tgt x pflip. Here tgt = engagement x PERS x (1+0.3 bpf) x delivery_mult, weighted by IMP. Structurally this is a profit-aware objective whose per-member benefits are owner-set tables, not estimated valuations.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The analogy is partial. The optimizer allocates money that shifts per-member flip odds; it does not pick cascade seeds. So the survey's spread-objective guarantees do not apply, and the fixed-state concavity certificate is the system's own. The survey's point carries over directly: the result is only as good as the PERS and IMP valuations, which no literature here estimates. A uniform-benefit variant (cost-aware) would be a sensitivity check, not a replacement.

bearings.paper_claim: Most behaviour-aware methods still use conventional IC or LT diffusion. These may not emulate real spreading, and changing the diffusion model can significantly change accuracy. Simulation-based influence estimation is the most expensive family; RIS, MIA and centrality are cheaper.
bearings.system_side: Competitive IC with common random numbers (MC 20, scenario 40). Bystanders turn anti with probability min(0.9, industry$/400000), and the saturation constant is 6. None of these model choices has been checked against observed cosponsorship accumulation.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The survey gives no numbers, so this is only a caution that outputs are model-conditional. The compute ranking matters little at N=533. RIS for two-colour competitive IC is not standard, so cost is not a reason to switch. The binding issue is validation of the diffusion model, not speed.

gaps_exposed: No topic-conditioned edge probabilities: one cosponsor kernel serves all 18 CU categories (per_topic_coalition.py:37), whereas topic-aware IM treats topic-dependent influence as the realistic case.

The cascade has no signed (foe) edges. The LLM-valence reference layer and the signed-coalition partition exist but stay outside the kernel, and neither has a validation that it predicts reduced cosponsorship.

Per-member benefit valuations in the allocator (PERS, IMP, delivery_mult) are owner tables. The survey names unavailable valuations as the main weakness of profit-aware IM, and no uniform-benefit sensitivity run is recorded.
No adaptive-diffusion feedback: the survey's research direction feeds behaviour changes back into spread, while stance dynamics stay a separate proposals-only module whose co-movement test was null.
No empirical check that IC or LT diffusion fits observed cosponsor join sequences, which the survey flags as a source of large accuracy changes.
flags: Citation overreach in code: receptivity_layer.py:29-31, budget_frontier.py:73 and outcome_contract.py:17 ('Chen/SNAM') cite this survey as grounds for contingency-aware seed activation. The survey is a taxonomy with no take-up estimates, and its four families do not include contingency-aware seeding as such. It supports only including member features, not the seed_prob magnitudes. Suggested wording: 'framing per Zareie & Sakellariou 2023; magnitudes are design priors, UNVERIFIED pending H1'.

Name collision: Paul's position for melange-sna.co-appearance-and-references cites 'Zareie & Sakellariou 2020' (similarity-based link prediction), which is a different paper from this 2023 IM survey. The two should not be conflated in notes or citations.

Any move to trust-aware (signed) cascade edges based on this survey would be new agent analysis and stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062). The survey itself warns that numeric friend/foe encodings may not capture attitudes.

The survey's 'influence' and 'spread' are model outputs of IC or LT on online graphs. Using this vocabulary for member ranks or route scores must follow D-025: heuristic outputs, never access or introduction probabilities.
The paper does not argue for either rejected SNA proposal (dropping regular cosponsorship edges; per-edge volume normalization), so there is nothing to flag on that front.
rel.paul_alignment: Paul has no annotations on this paper, and it is not cited in his component positions; his co-appearance note cites the 2020 Zareie link-prediction paper instead. The survey still fits his stated direction. It supports behaviour-aware seeding, which is Paul's mapping of Chen's contingency-aware IM to legislators who may not move when approached. It also matches his call to model rival industries and sign, and his emphasis on directionality. It qualifies his receptivity ambitions without contradicting them. The survey's own challenges (silent users, crude numeric attitude encodings, model sensitivity) echo the system's poor validity record for trait-based receptivity, which his notes underweight. His GCOMB and learned-policy expectations sit in the behaviour-agnostic tier, which this survey deliberately excludes. The system cites this paper more strongly than its content supports: in code it stands as a basis for seed_prob, which is a design prior.

related.why: The code pairs the two papers ('Chen/SNAM') for seed_prob. Chen supplies the contingency-aware seeding model; this survey supplies only the behaviour-aware framing.
Same authors, different task (latent-tie link prediction). Paul's notes cite the 2020 paper for the signed reference layer, so the two must be kept distinct.
Trust-aware IM needs signed edges. Leskovec gives the method for predicting positive and negative links that such a kernel would need.
Negative link inference is the data prerequisite for the friend/foe IM family the survey reviews.
The competitive IC behind Melange's two-colour cascade is outside this survey's behaviour-aware scope. Bharathi covers the competitive side.
Voter-dynamics influence maximization is an opinion-aware formulation of the kind the survey groups under opinion dynamics, and it is already cited for the contested-bills counterparty term.
A behaviour-agnostic, embedding-based IM method from the family this survey explicitly excludes and defers to earlier surveys.
The survey's tables separate simple from complex spreading. Chen's complex-contagion IM is the complex-spreading counterpart to Melange's LT priming.
